title: Paid to Play With Puzzles
text:
Around 1970 the psychologist Edward Deci, then a graduate student at Carnegie Mellon, brought college students into a lab to work on a puzzle called Soma, a set of oddly shaped plastic blocks that can be fitted together into many figures. Students tended to find it absorbing and fun. Each person came for three sessions and was shown drawings of shapes to reproduce.

In the middle session, half of the students were paid a dollar for each puzzle they solved. The other half did the same puzzles without pay. In the first and third sessions, nobody was paid.

The key moment came during a break in each session. The experimenter left the room for eight minutes, saying he needed to enter data, and the student was free to do anything: read magazines on the table, rest, or keep playing with the puzzles. Hidden observers recorded how long they spent on the puzzles. Students who had been paid in the second session spent less of their free time on the puzzles in the third session, once the money stopped, than students who had never been paid. The unpaid students showed no such drop. Deci concluded that paying people for something they already enjoyed could shift why they did it.
lesson: Money can crowd out the joy people find in their work. When people already care about a task, lead with autonomy and meaning, not only with rewards.
source: Deci, E. L. (1971). Effects of externally mediated rewards on intrinsic motivation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 18(1), 105-115.
caveat: The undermining effect has held up in meta-analyses for expected, task-contingent rewards, but it is weaker or absent for unexpected rewards and for dull tasks.
